---
title: "Part 3 — Working as a group"
---

This is the part that actually matters. Everything before it was single-player.

## 1. Everyone else joins: clone

Each other group member does this once.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Clone github.com/OUR-GROUP/penguin-clinic into my projects folder.
:::

```bash
cd ~/projects
git clone https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic.git
```

Then open `penguin-clinic.Rproj` in RStudio. You have a complete copy: every
file, and the entire history. A clone already knows where it came from, so
`git push` and `git pull` work immediately with no setup.

::: {.callout-note}
## Clone once, pull forever
Cloning again because "it stopped working" is the student equivalent of
reinstalling Windows. You almost never need to.
:::

## 2. The contribution cycle

This is the loop for every piece of work, all term. Five steps.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    P["<b>1. pull</b><br/>get everyone's latest work"] --> B["<b>2. branch</b><br/>start your own line of work"]
    B --> C["<b>3. commit</b><br/>as often as you like, locally"]
    C --> PR["<b>4. push + open a Pull Request</b><br/>ask your group to take your work"]
    PR --> M["<b>5. a teammate merges,<br/>then everyone pulls</b>"]
    M --> P
```

### Step 1 & 2 — pull, then branch

```bash
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c feature/describe-by-sex
```

Branch names: `feature/what-it-does`. Not `ulo`, not `new`, not `test2`.
Someone reading the pull request list in three weeks should know what each one
was for.

### Step 3 — work, and commit as you go

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Commit what I've done so far with a message about adding the sex-stratified
> summary table.
:::

Commit *often* and *small*. Every commit is a point you can return to. A
single commit called "did the whole analysis" is a point you can return to
only if you want to lose the whole analysis.

**Check your code runs before you commit.** In this project:

```bash
Rscript -e 'source("R/01-clean.R"); source("R/02-describe.R"); print(describe_by_sex(load_visits()))'
```

Real output:

``` text
        arm sex  n mean_score sd_score
1   control   F 26      60.32     6.06
2 treatment   F 25      56.08     6.02
3   control   M 34      60.77     6.33
4 treatment   M 35      54.76     7.67
```

### Step 4 — push the branch and open a Pull Request

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Push this branch and open a pull request explaining what I changed, why, and
> how a reviewer can check it.
:::

```bash
git push -u origin feature/describe-by-sex
gh pr create --base main --title "Add sex-stratified descriptives" --body "..."
```

A pull request worth reviewing answers three questions. Ours did:

> **What** — Adds `describe_by_sex()` in `R/02-describe.R` and shows the table
> in the Descriptives section.
>
> **Why** — The arms were balanced by construction (60/60) but sex was not, so
> the pooled table could hide a difference between strata.
>
> **How to check this** — `describe_by_sex(load_visits())`; expect 4 rows
> summing to n = 120.

That third heading is the one students skip and reviewers need most.

### Step 5 — a teammate reviews and merges

::: {.callout-important}
## You do not merge your own pull request
Someone else in the group opens it on GitHub, reads the diff, and presses
**Merge pull request → Squash and merge**.

Choose **Squash and merge**, not the default "Create a merge commit": it puts
exactly one commit on `main` per contribution, which makes `main`'s history
readable and makes undoing a bad contribution a single step.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why the example repository does not follow its own advice

If you look at the history of
[the example repository](https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic/commits/main),
you will find merge commits, not squashes. That is deliberate.

Squashing hides the branching. For *your* project that is exactly what you
want — a clean line of contributions on `main`. But for a repository whose job
is to *teach* branching, throwing the branches away would throw away the
lesson. Merge commits keep the shape visible:

``` text
*   76e5a30 Merge pull request #2
|\
| *   e9868fb Merge main into feature/limitations
| |\
|/|
* | 76c6037 Strengthen the synthetic-data disclaimer
| * b41c5d3 Note that the simulation guarantees correct specification
|/
*   929bf6e Merge student C's interpretation
|\
| * de43b31 Write the Interpretation section
* | b10d837 Add interpretation with estimate and CI
|/
*   32afb9c Merge pull request #1
|\
| * 26826f2 Add sex-stratified descriptives
|/
* 752e171 Set up project skeleton
```

Read from the bottom, that is every situation in this tutorial: a clean pull
request (#1), a conflict between two people sharing `main` (`929bf6e`), a
pull request that went stale because `main` moved on (`76c6037` vs `b41c5d3`),
and that conflict resolved inside the branch (`e9868fb`) before it was merged
(#2).

Try it yourself:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic.git
cd penguin-clinic
git log --oneline --graph
```

So: **squash in your own project, and read the example's graph to understand
what squashing would have hidden.**
:::

### The step everyone forgets

**Merging on GitHub does not change anything on your laptop.** Your local
`main` is now behind. Real output from this project immediately after the
merge:

``` text
* feature/describe-by-sex 26826f2 [origin/feature/describe-by-sex] Add sex-...
  main                    752e171 [origin/main] Set up project skeleton
```

Local `main` still points at the old commit. So after every merge, everyone
in the group runs:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> My PR was merged. Update my main and clean up the branch.
:::

```bash
git switch main
git pull
git fetch --prune                        # forget branches deleted on GitHub
git branch -d feature/describe-by-sex    # delete the local copy
```

Skip this and you will, a week later, commit new work onto a branch that was
merged and deleted, and be very confused.

## 3. The merge conflict, on purpose

Now the thing you are actually here for. Do this deliberately, in class, while
nothing is at stake.

**Setup.** Two group members both edit the **Interpretation** section of
`report.qmd` — the same lines — without pulling in between.

### What happens: student C pushes first

```bash
git commit -am "Write the Interpretation section"
git push
```

Fine. GitHub now has student C's paragraph.

### Student A, who did not pull, tries to push

```bash
git commit -am "Add interpretation with effect estimate and CI"
git push
```

Real output:

``` text
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/...'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing
hint: to the same ref. You may want to first integrate the remote changes
hint: (e.g., 'git pull ...') before pushing again.
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Read that hint. It is telling you the truth.

"The remote contains work that you do not have locally" means: **your teammate
pushed something and you would be overwriting it.** Git is refusing to let you
destroy their work.

There is a way to force it — `git push --force` — and it does exactly what it
sounds like: it deletes your teammate's commits from GitHub. Never type it.
If some website tells you to, that website is not thinking about your group.
:::

### So student A pulls

```bash
git pull
```

Real output:

``` text
Auto-merging report.qmd
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in report.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

`git status` tells you precisely what git wants:

``` text
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Unmerged paths:
	both modified:   report.qmd
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `git merge --abort` is your safety net
It puts everything back exactly as it was before the pull. If you panic, use
it. Nothing is lost. Then try again when you are calm.
:::

### Reading the conflict

Open `report.qmd` in RStudio. It contains both versions:

``` text
<<<<<<< HEAD
Treatment was associated with a lower score than control (adjusted
difference -5.23, 95% CI -7.53 to -2.94). We stress that these data are
simulated, so this is a demonstration of the estimator and not evidence
about any real intervention.
=======
In this simulated dataset the treatment arm scored about 5 points lower
than control after adjustment for age and sex. Because the data were
generated with a known arm effect of -4, the estimate is close to the
truth but not identical - ordinary sampling variation.
>>>>>>> de43b31
```

- `<<<<<<< HEAD` up to `=======` — **your** version
- `=======` down to `>>>>>>>` — **their** version
- `de43b31` — the ID of their commit

### Resolving it: the actual skill

Look at those two paragraphs. Student A has the numbers. Student C has the
comparison against the known simulated effect. **Neither is wrong, and each
says something the other omitted.** So the resolution keeps both:

``` markdown
Treatment was associated with a lower score than control (adjusted
difference -5.23 points, 95% CI -7.53 to -2.94). These data were simulated
with a known arm effect of -4, so the estimate is close to the truth but not
identical: the interval covers -4, and the gap between -5.23 and -4 is
ordinary sampling variation rather than bias.

This is a demonstration of the estimator on synthetic data. It is not
evidence about any real intervention.
```

::: {.callout-important}
## This is why you cannot fully delegate this

Ask Claude to resolve a conflict and it will produce something clean and
plausible. It may quietly pick one version, or blend them into a sentence your
group never agreed to claim. It does not know which number you decided to
report, or that you agreed last week to always flag the data as simulated.

**Delegate the mechanics, own the meaning.** A good prompt tells it the
decision:

> There's a conflict in the Interpretation section. Keep both points: my
> estimate with its confidence interval, and C's comparison against the known
> simulated effect of -4. Merge them into one paragraph and keep the sentence
> saying the data are synthetic.
:::

### Before you commit the resolution — two checks

1. **All markers gone?**

```bash
grep -nE '^(<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>)' report.qmd || echo "clean"
```

2. **Does it still run?** A half-resolved file is valid text and invalid code.

```bash
quarto render report.qmd
```

Skipping check 2 is how `<<<<<<< HEAD` ends up in a submitted report.

### Finish the merge

```bash
git add report.qmd
git commit -m "Merge student C's interpretation with the effect estimate"
git push
```

The history now shows exactly what happened:

``` text
*   929bf6e Merge student C's interpretation with the effect estimate
|\
| * de43b31 Write the Interpretation section        <- student C
* | b10d837 Add interpretation with estimate and CI <- student A
|/
*   32afb9c Merge pull request #1
```

Both people's work survives, and the record shows who wrote what and how it
was reconciled. That is the entire value proposition of git in one picture.

### And the other members pull

```bash
git pull
```

``` text
Updating de43b31..929bf6e
Fast-forward
 report.qmd | 12 ++++++++----
```

"Fast-forward" means there was nothing to reconcile — you simply moved
forward. Most pulls look like this. Conflicts are the exception, not the rule.

## 4. How to almost never have conflicts

Conflicts need **two people editing the same lines between pulls**. Break any
link in that chain:

1. **Own your files.** The README says who owns what. Stay in your file.
2. **Pull before you start. Push when you stop.** Shrinks the window.
3. **Small, frequent pull requests.** A branch alive for two weeks is a
   conflict with a countdown.
4. **In shared prose, one paragraph per person, on its own lines.** Conflicts
   are line-based, so blank lines between contributions genuinely help.
5. **Say out loud when you are about to touch a shared file.** The cheapest
   version-control tool is a group chat message.

## Next: the other kind of conflict

The conflict above happened because two people shared `main`. If your group
follows the pull-request discipline, you will more often meet a conflict that
shows up **on the pull request** instead — your push succeeds, and GitHub
tells you afterwards. That is [Part 3½](03b-pr-conflict.qmd), and the correct
fix points in the opposite direction.
